name: Ser Hollis Garrow
appearance: Sixty-one, broad, white-bearded and red in the face, with a voice that carries over the Wend in flood. His right leg is gone above the knee, lost at Harrow Ford; under his cot lies the leg the lay brothers made him, beech and a leather cup, which fits the way a boot fits someone else, and he took nine steps on it yesterday and swore at every one. He talks in a sergeant's rhythm, profane and warm, insults doing the work of affection, and has told Darrow to his face that his head is not as fast as his feet.
last_seen_doing: On his cot in the infirmary hall, pushing the folded writ from Harrow Ford, still unread, into the cup of his wooden leg while Benedek Orrin says his oath with his eyes shut, as a latch lifts down the hall and the cell door opens.
now: He lies in the infirmary hall of Saint Ysolde's, second on the list of the Faithless that the Confessors read out at the inn in Coldmere, with Benedek Orrin of his own Sixth on the next cot and the writ from Harrow Ford hidden, still unread, in the cup of the wooden leg under his cot. The Captain is shut in a cell down the hall with Mender Vorne, and nothing comes through that door; as the Interlude ends, it opens. Six grey cloaks and a cart are on the Holloway below, and if the snow holds off they will reach the foot of the Steps by tomorrow night.
story_so_far: At Harrow Ford he brought the writ from command that sent the Sixth and the Ninth into the river, and when Darrow pointed at the carts and children behind the clan line he answered that the clans were stupid and told him to mount up. He came back from Harrow Ford on a cart, missing his right leg above the knee. On the five days of carts and barge back through the Lowmarch, with the Crown's heralds reading the proclamation of the Faithless from every bell-house, he cursed everything from the surgeon to himself and then went quiet. He has had the cot next to Darrow's at Saint Ysolde's since, mostly drunk through the weeks before the Binding, and now six grey cloaks and a censer are on the Holloway below with his name second on their list.

quote.text: Nobody's taking anyone. Not up eleven hundred steps in the snow. They'll read their list at the bottom and freeze.

known_facts.fact: He commands the Sixth Lance, which was dressing its line a hundred yards downstream of the Ninth at Harrow Ford.
He carried the sealed writ from command ordering the Sixth and the Ninth to clear the ford with the Second in reserve, and broke its wax with his thumb without looking at it.

When Darrow pointed at the carts, old people and children behind the clan line and suggested the clans were coming through rather than at them, Hollis said they were stupid, that the writ said clear the ford, and that Darrow's head was not as fast as his feet.
He lost his right leg above the knee at Harrow Ford.

On the road back he cursed for five days without repeating himself once: the surgeon, the river, the Crown, the clans, the oxen, the weather, the carter, Darrow, and finally himself, which was when he went quiet.
His answer to the Crown's proclamation, which offered the Faithless mercy at the Oathspire and leave to kneel anew, was "Kneel to that," and nobody on either cart laughed.
He kept the cot next to Darrow's through the six weeks before the Binding, mostly drunk, and offered commentary.
He knew the grey cloaks and the smoking censer on the Holloway for Confessors before anyone else said the word, and his face went the color of the window.
His name is second on the list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's that was read out at the inn in Coldmere; asked who was first, Wren did not answer and looked at Darrow.

He can say the order from Harrow Ford with his eyes shut, and has kept the paper folded small inside his shirt, wax inward, against his ribs; he has not looked at the seal since he broke it on the west bank.
The lay brothers made him a leg of beech and a leather cup, which fits the way a boot fits someone else; he took nine steps on it and swore at every one.
He has not had a drink in two days, meant to tell somebody, and could not think who.

When Benedek Orrin of his own Sixth asked what second on the list meant and whether they would take him down, he said nobody was taking anyone up eleven hundred steps in the snow, and that they would read their list at the bottom and freeze.
For a fortnight he has thought of the Captain with a sword and a chair under him: a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.

He told Benedek to say his oath and shut his eyes, and while the lad's lips moved he pushed the folded writ, still unread, into the cup of the wooden leg, where no Confessor would think to look; he has been telling himself since midsummer that he will look at the wax later.

relationships.label: the captain on the next cot
relationships.note: He brought Darrow the writ at Harrow Ford and told him to mount up, rode the next cart over on the road back, has had the next cot at Saint Ysolde's since, and now stands second on a list on which Wren, asked who was first, only looked at Darrow. For a fortnight he has thought of the Captain fighting from a chair, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.

relationships.label: the girl with the ledger who brought word of the list
relationships.note: She was the one who brought word of the grey cloaks and the censer on the Holloway, and who told him his name stood second on the list.

relationships.label: the lad on the next cot, of his own Sixth
relationships.note: Not yet thirty, a boar spear through the shoulder at the ford and a fever after it; he asked Hollis what second on the list meant, offered to carry him down the Steps himself, and was told he couldn't carry a bucket, which made him smile, which was what the words were for.

fire.state: the Grace is gone; nothing kindled in its place
